title: TEMP.Veles
summary: TEMP.Veles, reported by Dragos under the name Xenotime, is an activity cluster that public reporting links to intrusions into industrial control system environments, most notably at a petrochemical plant in the Middle East, with additional activity reported in Europe and North America. The distinguishing feature was not broad malware but purpose built tooling designed to interact with the safety instrumented systems that monitor and shut down dangerous industrial processes, combined with a determined effort to reach those networks from information technology environments. Dragos described the group as a development effort with strong operational security rather than a large campaign, and attribution to a state linked nexus was offered as an assessment. The defensible lesson is architectural: safety systems should be separated from business networks, remote access into operational technology should be tightly controlled, and engineers should watch for unexpected engineering workstation traffic.

beginner.definition: TEMP.Veles is a name for attackers who broke into industrial control networks. These are the computers that run factories, power plants and pipelines. Public reports describe a focus on safety systems that can shut a dangerous process down. One security company calls the same activity Xenotime. Researchers believe a state sponsor supported the work, but they present that as a judgement rather than a proven fact.
beginner.whyItMatters: When attackers reach industrial systems, the result can be physical damage or danger to workers. These networks were often built to be reliable, not to resist an intruder. Safety systems are the last line of defence, so they must be isolated from everyday business networks. Engineers and security teams also need to talk to each other, because signs of intrusion may look like a normal process change.
howItWorks: The attackers get into the normal business network first, often through email or a weak service.
They then search for connections that lead toward the factory or the plant network.
They then steal the credentials for engineering workstations, jump hosts and remote access gateways.
They install tools that are made specifically for the industrial devices they find.
They then learn how the safety system monitors and controls the whole industrial process.
They prepare changes that could damage equipment or stop production for a long time.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital where the front desk and the operating theatre share one corridor. A thief who talks his way past the front desk is already close to the theatre doors. Hospitals build separate entrances and locked doors for a reason. In the same way, factory control rooms need their own locked path, separate from the busy public corridor of office computers.
takeaways: Keep industrial and safety networks separate from normal business networks.
Control and record every remote connection into plant systems.
Signs of an incident may look like a change in the physical process.

objectives: Explain what industrial control systems are and why they differ from office networks.
Describe the role of network separation between business and plant environments.
Explain why safety systems are a priority target in this kind of intrusion.
Identify the evidence that suggests movement from information technology to plant networks.
Explain how engineering and security teams should cooperate during an incident.
